metadata.note: STEM/AI explainer, week 11. Every figure computed in this session by running fuse's optimizer and runtime on resnet18 exported per the repo's data/export.sh, plus onnxruntime as an independent reference and a double-precision check of the fold algebra.

beats.new_visual_element: Hesitant writer, the assumption corrected on screen
beats.narration: I built a small compiler that rewrites neural networks so they run leaner. Every rewrite comes with a promise that the answers did not change. That promise comes from the same tool that made the change, so I did not want to take its word for it.
beats.narration_text: I built a small compiler that rewrites neural networks so they run leaner. Every rewrite comes with a promise that the answers did not change. That promise comes from the same tool that made the change, so I did not want to take its word for it.

props.text:
My optimizer
says nothing
changed.
I can trust it.

beats.narration: On resnet18, an image model exported with all its clutter left in, the compiler takes 141 operations down to 32. It removes 72 pass-through nodes, folds all 20 normalization layers into the convolutions before them, and fuses 17 activations.

beats.narration: The fold is where a whole layer disappears. A normalization layer takes the convolution's output, shifts it and rescales it. Both steps are linear, so they can be folded back into the convolution's own weights and bias, once, ahead of time. One operation does the work of two.

props.title: Fold the normalization into the weights
props.note: Shift and rescale are linear, so they fold into the weights once, before the model runs.
props.conditions: Checked on the first layer in double precision: both forms agree to 14 decimal places.

beats.narration: To check it, I ran the same image through the original network and the rewritten one and compared all one thousand outputs. The largest difference was about one millionth, on outputs as large as 4.7, and the top prediction was the same. A millionth is rounding, not the rewrite.

beats.narration: But both runs used my own runtime, and a broken runtime would agree with itself perfectly. So before trusting either result, I had checked my runtime against onnxruntime, an engine I did not write. They agree to about two millionths, with the same top prediction.

beats.narration: What I keep: a report from a tool is a claim. Run both versions and compare, and check your checker against something that does not share its mistakes. It is the same rule I follow when the textbook's audit and its evidence disagree.

The last millionth is rounding, not the rewrite.
Check the checker against an outside engine.
